title: Is It True That If I Were Dead You Would Feel
text:
Is it true that, were I dead, you would feel

less life in yourself without mine?

That the sun would not shine as before,

knowing me in the night of the tomb?


What astonishment, my love, when I saw

all that in your letter! I am yours...

But... do I matter to you so much? How can I

serve you wine with my trembling hand?


I will renounce the dreams of death,

returning to the miseries of living.

Love me, love, your breath resurrects!


Others exchanged their rank for love,

and I for you the tomb, the heavenly

sweetness for earth here with you.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the speaker's startled return from death-dreams into earthly love.

title: How Do I Love You? Well, I Love You...
text:
How do I love you? Well, I love you

to the abyss and to the highest region

I can reach when I pursue

the limits of Being and the Ideal.


I love you in the most everyday living,

with the sun and by candlelight.

With freedom, as one aspires to Good;

with the innocence of one who longs for glory.


I love you with the fever I once put

into my grief and with my childhood faith,

with the love I thought I lost


when I lost my saints... With the tears

and smiles of my life... And if God wills,

I will love you much more after death.
editorial_note: This first-line variant keeps the same English rendering as the matching Browning sonnet.

title: If You Must Love Me
text:
If you must love me, let it be only

for love of my love. Never say

that it is for my appearance, my smile, the melody

of my voice, or for my gentle character


that agrees with yours, or that on that day

made us feel happy...

For, my love, all these things

may change, and even love dies.


Do not love me either for the tears

you compassionately wipe from my face...

For I may forget to weep


thanks to you, and so lose your love!

For love of my love I want you to love me,

so that it may dwell in heaven, eternally.
editorial_note: The translation follows the Spanish version's insistence on love grounded only in love itself.

title: Love, Just Because It Is Love
text:
And nevertheless love, just because it is love,

is beautiful. A great temple and the grass

flame equally bright. The same fire

burns, consuming cedar and tares.


And love is a fire; and when I say

I love you, oh God, I love you, before your eyes

I am transfigured into splendor and feel

my dazzling face flash.


In love there can be no meanness,

even though the meanest beings love,

for when they love God, He accepts them.


And in the mean appearance of what I am,

the feeling shines and purifies

what is flesh because it is the fruit of love.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the theological argument that love purifies even flesh and lowliness.

title: Grief
text:
I tell you that grief without hope is grief without passion,

and that only unbelieving men feel pain,

snatched up by anguish, in the night air,

rising toward God's throne shouting spells.

A desert full of souls, naked silence lies

beneath the snowy, vertical eye of absolute Heaven.

The deep-hearted man expresses grief

for his dead in the quietest silence, mute,

like an enormous statue raised in eternal stone,

not moving until he himself lies in the earth.

Touch them: the marble of their eyes never grows wet,

for if it could weep, it might arise and disappear.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the severe meditation on grief, silence, and unmoving marble.
